title: The Generator Ban That Sent Sunil Mittal to a Taiwan Phone Fair
dek: When India banned the generator imports his trade depended on, a young Ludhiana businessman went looking for something new and found the push-button phone.

story.event: Losing his generator import trade to a ban and turning to push-button telephones
story.summary: In the early 1980s Sunil Bharti Mittal, who had started with a bicycle crankshaft unit in Ludhiana in 1976, lost his large business importing Suzuki portable generators when India licensed two domestic manufacturers and banned imports. Refused a Maruti car dealership, he searched Japan, Korea and Taiwan for a new product and, at a Taiwanese trade fair he dates to October 1982, found the push-button telephone, which he imported as parts and assembled in India. Telephone equipment led Bharti to bid for a mobile licence in 1992 and to launch Airtel in Delhi in the mid-1990s.
paragraphs: In the early 1980s Sunil Bharti Mittal was in his twenties and, by his own account, the world's largest importer of portable generators from Japan. He sold Suzuki sets through small offices in four Indian cities to households that wanted power during electricity cuts. Then two Indian companies were licensed to make generators at home, and the government banned imports to protect them. He could not land another shipment. "Overnight, I had no business," he recalled in 2017.

It was not his first change of course. He had started in Ludhiana in 1976, aged 18, with about $1,500 borrowed from his father, forging bicycle crankshafts for the town's cycle makers. He left because the buyers set the price and, as he later put it, "just making shafts wouldn't have made you a player of any size or scale." Trading in steel, zip fasteners and plastics had led him to Suzuki. Now, the journalist Vir Sanghvi reported, Suzuki recommended him for a dealership for the new Maruti car, and he was turned down.

So he went looking for something nobody in India was doing yet, because, he said, competing with established firms on their own ground gave him no chance. In Japan, video recorders and colour televisions did not appeal; in Seoul nothing clicked. At a trade fair in Taiwan, which he dates to October 1982, he saw a push-button telephone for the first time. India still dialled on rotary phones, and finished sets could not be imported, so he had them broken into parts in Taiwan and reassembled at home. Sanghvi wrote that Mittal admitted those early imports may well have been illegal. He sold them as Mitbrau, a name meant to sound foreign; it stood for Mittal brothers.

Telephones became the business. Bharti built a phone factory in Ludhiana, a town not known for electronics, and its Beetel brand added cordless phones, answering machines and fax machines. That knowledge, Mittal said, is what made him bid in 1992 for one of India's first mobile licences against far larger groups. After court challenges, Bharti took the Delhi licence and launched Airtel there in the mid-1990s. Of the lost dealership he told Sanghvi: "Looking back, I think that it was God's design that I should not get too comfortable."

quote.text: to condemn them as impossible, is by a temerarious presumption to pretend to know the utmost bounds of possibility.
quote.locator: Book I, Chapter XXVI, "That it is folly to measure truth and error by our own capacity"
quote.translator: Charles Cotton (1685), ed. W. C. Hazlitt
quote.source_title: Essays of Michel de Montaigne — Complete, tr. Charles Cotton, Project Gutenberg eBook #3600
quote.connection: Montaigne warns against calling a thing impossible merely because it is unfamiliar. In India at the time the push-button phone was almost unknown, and Mittal read that as an opening rather than a limit, the same habit that later carried him into the mobile licence bid.

reflection: Two doors closed on Mittal within a short time: a rule that ended his trade, and a dealership that went to someone else. He called the second one fortunate only looking back, years later. At the time it was simply a refusal.

You work in a field where rules and approvals can shift the ground under you, and where some doors close for reasons that have little to do with the quality of your work. It is fine not to find meaning in a closed door straight away. What Mittal did in the meantime was practical: he travelled, looked, and kept asking what was not yet being done.
invitation: Write down one useful thing that nobody around you is doing yet, however small, and leave the note alone until you have rested.

cross_checks.claim: Mittal started in 1976 making bicycle crankshafts with about $1,500 borrowed capital
The government banned generator imports after licensing Indian manufacturers, ending his generator trade
Searching for a new product, Mittal found push-button telephones at a trade fair in Taiwan
Bharti bid for a mobile licence in 1992 and won the Delhi circle

research_notes: Dates of the ban and the Taiwan trip disagree: Mittal (HBS oral history, 2017) puts the Taiwan trade fair in October 1982, after the ban; Vir Sanghvi dates the domestic licences and the import ban to 1983; Dataquest (2002, which blocks automated requests and is not cited) says he brought push-button phones to India in 1982. The story says 'the early 1980s' for the ban and gives October 1982 as Mittal's own date for the fair. Where he saw the phone: Mittal (HBS, Wharton) and Sanghvi say a Taiwan trade fair; MBA Review (2009) says a roadside hawker in Singapore; the story follows Mittal. Starting capital: Wharton and MBA Review give $1,500 borrowed from his father; Dataquest gives Rs 20,000; the story uses $1,500. Where he moved: Mittal says Mumbai (HBS, Wharton) around 1979-80, while Sanghvi says he moved to his father's MP flat in Delhi in 1979; the story avoids naming the city. Legality: Sanghvi writes the component imports were illegal 'as far as I can tell' and that Mittal did not need to admit they 'may well have been illegal', implying that he did; the story attributes this to Sanghvi. Mobile launch: Mittal says '94, '95; the story says the mid-1990s. The Siemens technical tie-up is dated 1985 by Dataquest and 1986 by MBA Review and is left out. The HBS transcript PDF is linked from the cited page through an expiring signed link, so the stable page URL is given. Sanghvi's profile is undated on his site; a comment stamp suggests about 2005. Montaigne's sentence concerns reports of unlikely events; it is applied by analogy.
